title: Deferred execution and hot-path traps
hook: On a 199-to-999 concurrent attempt-submit path, enumerating the same filtered query twice is two CPU passes and two different snapshots if the list is still growing.

sections.heading: Immediate versus deferred, streaming versus buffering
sections.prose: Operators that return a scalar (Count, Any, First, Max, Sum) execute immediately. Operators that return IEnumerable typically defer. Deferred operators split into streaming (Where, Select, SelectMany, Take) and non-streaming (OrderBy, GroupBy, Reverse). Streaming yields as it reads. Buffering reads everything first. ToList and ToArray freeze a snapshot. Microsoft’s classification table is the thing to cite, not a vague “LINQ is lazy.”

snippets.label: Double enumeration on a live submit buffer
snippets.explanation: Count and foreach each run Where. Inserts between them change the report. ToList once is the hot-path fix.

sections.heading: Captured variables and accidental work
sections.prose: The query closes over cutoff, tenantId, and sometimes this. Changing cutoff after the query is built and before it is enumerated uses the new value — deferred by design. In high concurrency, that is a race unless the captured locals are snapshots. Chaining two Where clauses is still one pass when you finally enumerate; chaining Where after ToList is a second pass on a copy. Logging .ToList() in a diagnostic build inside a library method that then returns IEnumerable surprises callers who enumerate again.

snippets.label: Capture of a loop variable that moves
snippets.explanation: Without id, every query would see the final tenantCount value (C# no longer has the old foreach capture bug for foreach, but for-loop ints still need a copy if you close over the iterator).

interviewTakeaways: Declaration is a plan; enumeration is work.
Scalar operators and ToList/ToArray are immediate; most sequence operators defer.
GroupBy/OrderBy defer but buffer; they are not cheap streaming.
Enumerate once on hot paths; snapshot captured filters.
commonPitfalls: Calling Count then foreach on the same IEnumerable.
Returning a query over a using-disposed enumerator (yield after dispose).
Putting expensive Select lambdas in a query that reporting enumerates three times.

jsTsCorrelations.note: array.filter is eager. JS iterators and generator pipelines are the deferred analogue. LINQ to Objects is closer to a generator chain than to Array.prototype.
A JS generator is lazy like IEnumerable until you spread it. Spreading twice re-runs the generator if you still have it.
